office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The district: East Gibson School Corporation covers Barton, Center and Columbia townships in eastern Gibson County, including Oakland City, Francisco, Mackey, Somerville and Buckskin [24]. It now operates Wood Memorial Primary, Wood Memorial Intermediate, Wood Memorial Middle and Wood Memorial High schools, with its central office in Oakland City [25]. Enrollment was 653 in October 2025 and 641 in January 2026, and the district projected 645 students for 2026–27 [26, 27]. Dr. Michael Galvin has been superintendent since 2024; the board gave him a two-year contract through June 2028 in July 2026 [28, 29].

The board has five members: Steve Sevier (president), Josh Brewer (vice president), Lynn Rowe (secretary), Roger Sermersheim and Lincoln Edwards [30, 31]. Members are elected from numbered districts; county results show Districts 1, 3 and 5 on the 2018 and 2022 ballots, District 2 in 2020 and 2024 and District 4 in 2020 [32, 33, 34, 35]. The Daily Clarion describes the 2026 seats as District 1 (Barton Township), District 3 (Oakland City) and District 5 (at-large) [36].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: three seats, each electing one member, matching the state list [36, 6]. All three current holders are running again: Sevier, elected unopposed in District 1 in 2018 and 2022, faces Joshua Hugh Maikranz; Brewer, who won District 3 in 2022 by one vote (162 to 161 over Orbie Day, with Rebecca S. Frederick third in the precinct totals summed by this guide), is unopposed; and Rowe, who won the District 5 at-large seat in 2022 over incumbent Steven Schenks (945 to 683, summed precinct totals), is unopposed [32, 33, 37].

Budget and SEA 1 (2026): Galvin told the board June 8, 2026 that SEA 1 will cost the district about $400,000 over three years but that budgeting and the closing of Francisco Elementary let the district absorb the loss, saying 'We are very far from closing our doors' [38]. The board approved a 2027 budget in August that Galvin said is 'very near what it was last year,' and the October 13, 2026 agenda lists final approval of the 2027 budget [27, 30].

Textbooks and insurance (July 2026): Galvin said the end of state textbook reimbursement, while the ban on textbook fees remains, leaves the district paying about $250,000 for K–8 textbooks; the board also approved a new employee health insurance bid that is still more than $12,000 above the prior year [29].

Custodial outsourcing (January–May 2026): citing state funding cuts and SEA 1, the board sought bids to contract out custodial work; union members and supporters urged the board to keep the unionized staff [39, 40]. After bids ranging from $484,584 to $948,682, compared with about $515,691 now spent, the board decided April 13 to keep its custodians, and approved a contract with them May 11 running through June 2030 [41, 42].

Enrollment and school choice: in his January 2026 State of the Schools report Galvin called enrollment a main challenge, reporting that 195 students who live in the district attend school elsewhere while 47 come in from outside, and that state dollars tied to enrollment are down more than $2 million over a decade [26].

Consolidation: Galvin told the board in April 2026 that 'The state is moving and pushing towards consolidation,' citing a bill directing the Department of Education to evaluate school corporations, and said in June that the only way the district would close is if legislators forced consolidation [41, 38].

Facilities: the board approved up to $232,150 for new gym bleachers in March 2026, hired a firm in May to do a $15,000 facilities audit of all buildings, and is holding off on some projects until the audit is done [43, 42, 27]. The 2027 capital projects plan lists roofing, flooring and parking lot projects and rooftop HVAC units [44]. In August the board bought a 0.16-acre lot across from campus for parking for $15,000 from board member Lincoln Edwards, who abstained; Sevier said Edwards had bought and cleared the burned property so the school could acquire it for what he had put into it [27].

Safety and policies: in February 2026 the board unanimously approved a visitor management system that checks visitors against the sex offender registry, an anonymous reporting system, new defibrillators and classroom bleeding-control kits [45]. For 2026–27 the district barred student cell phones for the full day, including lunch, and ended suspensions for excessive tardies [38].

Academics and programs (2026): the board adopted McGraw Hill reading (Wonders) for elementary grades and StudySync for middle school language arts, started a construction trades program, and planned a free dual-credit 'College Core' pilot with Indiana University [41, 42, 46, 38].
Board pay: in February 2026 the board raised member stipends from $2,000 to $4,500 a year, the first increase in at least 25 years; Rowe cast the only no vote [40].
Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum, questionnaire or campaign coverage for this race.

background: Elected without opposition in District 1 in 2018 and 2022 (as Stephen Joseph Sevier and Stephen J. Sevier) [32, 33].
Board president; the board lists a Fort Branch mailing address for him [30, 31].

items: On the custodial outsourcing study, said in January 2026 that the board was 'in the investigative stages' and that cutbacks were due to factors including state budget cuts: 'If we don't research it we don't know' [39].
Told a resident in February 2026 the board would not necessarily accept the lowest cleaning bid [40].

Explained the August 2026 parking-lot land purchase from board member Lincoln Edwards, saying Edwards bought and cleared the burned property because acquiring and demolishing it directly would have been difficult for the school [27].
